extracted.intended_audience: legislators, political philosophers, and students of political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for framing laws, constitutions, and institutions for a polis (city-state), focusing on property, education, magistracy, population, and military considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of non-citizen classes (slaves, Helots, Penestise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator must determine whether and how to give attention to dependants, slaves, Helots, Penestise, etc., including their polity, education, and laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglecting these groups makes them 'far more troublesome and high-spirited' and can produce revolt; their management is of no small consequence and not easy to determine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for communal wives and property
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making wives (or property) common without resolving the domestic management problems that arise from such communal arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making wives common while property remains separate raises questions of who will manage domestic concerns; making both common is also problematic and comparisons with animals are absurd. Legislators must ensure household care and family association are preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid permanent magistracy monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not arrange magistracies so that persons of the same rank are always in office; perpetual incumbency breeds sedition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed occupancy denies rotation of honor/power and can produce unrest especially among courageous or warlike citizens; offices should not be monopolized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure happiness across classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator ought to make all the citizens happy; a political arrangement is defective if any major class (notably the military) is unhappy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is not additive between persons; it must exist in the individual. If the military are unhappy, the state cannot claim universal happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility of political hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Political schemes and numerical proposals must be feasible given the country's resources (avoid requiring unreal resources like 'the country of Babylonia' to support idle persons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses should not be mere abstractions; a legislator must consider whether a plan is practicable in his territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame laws to the country, people, and neighbours
rubrics_metrics.description: When framing laws the legislator must have special regard to the country and the people, and also consider neighbouring states if political intercourse is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military practice and other arrangements should be adapted to local geography and to dealings with neighbours; neglecting these leads to inadequate preparation for war and diplomacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine property allotments precisely and adequately
rubrics_metrics.description: Property quantities should be more determinate than 'enough to live moderately'; aim for provision that encourages living both moderately and liberally to avoid luxury or wretchedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous phrasing invites extremes; property rules should connect to virtues (prudence, liberality) rather than merely numeric sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for population dynamics in property laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Property regulation must consider population increase, child mortality, and sterility; failing to regulate numbers alongside property can produce poverty and sedition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An equality of goods that ignores demographic change will collapse or cause many to be deprived; legislators should set limits on population or match property rules to expected demographic trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality of housing allotments
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid impractical rules such as allotting two separate houses to each person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation must consider everyday convenience and habitability — impractical arrangements undermine compliance and welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mixed/balanced constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect or 'most perfect' government is often a mixture of several forms (monarchy, oligarchy, democracy) blended together rather than a pure single form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blending many parts tends to produce the best constitution; simply mixing democracy and tyranny or poorly combining elements may yield the worst regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design electoral mechanics to avoid oligarchic bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Electoral rules (compulsion to vote for certain ranks, class-based arrangements) that favor the rich or a particular rank incline the state toward oligarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsory voting for only higher classes and exemptions for others will produce assemblies dominated by wealthier classes, especially when attendance among commonalty is low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent self-perpetuating electoral cliques
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid systems where elected persons subsequently choose other office-holders, as small combinations can then control outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing the elected to select new members concentrates power and enables factional control; election design should limit such clique formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of property equality
rubrics_metrics.description: If equality of goods is proposed it must be neither excessive (enabling luxury) nor too meagre (forcing hardship); equality limited to land is insufficient because other chattels matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators should define a proper medium of wealth, consider all forms of substance (land, slaves, cattle, money), and set realistic bounds (e.g., Plato's fivefold limit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education to produce common sentiments over material equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of sentiments among citizens is more important than mere equality of circumstances; education under law should cultivate shared dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property leveling alone is ineffective unless paired with an educational program that prevents greed and excessive ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address causes of theft/crime by provision, temperance, and philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent crimes arising from necessity, luxury, or desire: (1) supply moderate subsistence; (2) inculcate temperance; (3) provide philosophical/other outlets for pleasure-seeking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different causes of theft require different remedies — material provision, moral regulation, and cultural/philosophical avenues respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance wealth to military security and foreign temptations
rubrics_metrics.description: The state's wealth should not tempt stronger neighbours to invade nor be so meagre that the state cannot wage war with equals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property and economic policy must be set with military exigencies in mind — avoid making a polity a desirable prey or militarily impotent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial decision-making should be clear and not fragmentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should avoid splitting verdicts across claims in ways that turn them into arbitrators or force perjury; acquittal or condemnation should be decisively expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems that have judges write split tablets for different parts of an indictment encourage inconsistent judgments and confusion; judicial procedure should aim for coherent, accountable verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about rewarding informers and incentives for denunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewards for those who 'find out anything for the good of the city' risk encouraging informers and causing commotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While incentivizing beneficial discovery may seem attractive, it can erode trust and provoke instability if it promotes denunciation rather than genuine civic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law reform: weigh adaptability against the authority of custom
rubrics_metrics.description: While laws sometimes must be altered as arts progress, altering laws too readily weakens their power, since law derives strength from established custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, trifling advantages do not justify easy repeal; consider who may change laws, in what governments, and the broader consequences before permitting frequent amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate women's roles to preserve social order
rubrics_metrics.description: The indulgence or unmanaged liberties of women undermines the restraint of law (half the city unregulated) and can increase esteem for riches and disrupt military virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators must supervise women's conduct and roles; neglect can transfer power through women to others and produce disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection, duties, and integrity of major magistrates (ephori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates who handle matters of last importance should not be chosen accidentally from the whole populace nor be so susceptible to bribery; they should decide by law or custom, not private discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electing very poor or random persons to powerful offices risks corruption and tyranny; magistrates' way of life should be consistent with the city's manners and constrained by written laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align population incentives with land and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that reward childbearing must be compatible with land division and resources; otherwise, population incentives can produce many poor citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incentives (exemptions from duties for parents of many children) should be assessed against the ability of the land and economy to support increased numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating excluded or resentful classes by role division
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividing citizens into artisans, husbandmen, and soldiers but denying arms, land, or governance to some creates classes that feel like slaves to the soldiery and will not love the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that each class has a legitimate stake, share of honour or compensation, and routes to political attachment to prevent hostility and instability.
